Une voyelle suivie de deux consonnes est toujours accentuée: kisōnso, forêt [...] 5. Les syllabes qui résultent d'une contraction sont accentuées — pakēza (= pakaiza) lorsqu'il viendra. 6. Mais on dira: kukēnta (2de Règle), regarder [...] 7. Dans les mots de deux syllabes, c'est la première qui porte l'accent: būle, éleusine; lēta, apporte; pīta, passe; kōnu, ici.
new_statements.translation: It is supremely important to place the tonic accent correctly if one wants to be understood. The following rules are ranked by importance [i.e. an earlier rule overrides a later one] ... 2. A vowel followed by two consonants is always accented: kisōnso 'forest' ... 5. Syllables resulting from a contraction are accented — pakēza (= pakaiza) 'when he comes'. 6. In words of three syllables or more, the accent is on the antepenultimate: kusākana 'to meet', bīkusi 'grass', kitupīkilo 'lid'. But one says kukēnta (2nd rule) 'to look' ... 7. In words of two syllables it is the first that bears the accent: būle 'eleusine', lēta 'bring', pīta 'pass', kōnu 'here'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ranked rules: a vowel before a consonant cluster (NC) or a vowel arising from contraction always carries the 'accent'; otherwise the accent falls on the antepenultimate syllable in words of three or more syllables and on the first (= penultimate) syllable of disyllables; the final syllable of a word never bears it (Van Acker 1907 rule 1). Enclitic pronouns pull the accent onto the syllable immediately preceding them; monosyllables are long or short depending on the following word.
new_statements.exceptions: Rule ranking produces the exceptions: kukēnta not *kūkenta (cluster rule beats antepenult rule); reduplicated stems accent each half separately (kipōlopōlo, katyētye); disyllables closely bound to a preceding word lose their accent to that word's final syllable (letā bule 'bring the eleusine', pitā konu 'pass this way'); a vowel before another vowel (and y, w) is always short/unaccented; monosyllable length depends on the next word's first syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rules stated for citation forms, with explicit phrase-level adjustments (rules 3, 7, 8: enclitics and close-knit word groups shift the accent). Caveat: the author's 'accent tonique' is notated as vowel length (macron vs breve) and rules 1, 2, 5, 8 coincide exactly with the vowel-length neutralisation contexts of the modern descriptions (Ntambo 1984, Kalenga 1992, Kavimbwa 2002), which analyse Kitaabwa suprasegmentals as contrastive length + four tones and make no stress statement; the antepenult default (rule 6) is the only part not reducible to length.
new_statements.identity_note: de Beerst 1896 and Van Acker 1907 describe the Kitabwa of the Marungu highlands (White Fathers missions Mpala / Baudouinville-Kirungu, west shore of Lake Tanganyika, DR Congo) = core Taabwa M41 (taab1238). Kavimbwa 2002 labels his variety 'kitaabwa (M41a)', also DRC. Kalenga 1992 describes Shila (parler de Nkuba, Lake Mweru), which Glottolog files under taab1238 but which is sometimes treated as a distinct variety; it was used here only as corroboration (tone + length, no stress statement). Zambian Tabwa (Kaputa/Nsama districts) is not separately described in anything opened.

sources.note: Notions préliminaires § III 'L'Accent Tonique' (pp. 16-17): eight ranked rules. 1 V before V always short; 2 V before two consonants always accented (kisōnso); 3 enclitic pronouns draw accent onto the preceding syllable; 4 reduplicated stems accent each half as if isolated; 5 syllables from contraction accented (pakēza < pakaiza); 6 words of 3+ syllables: accent on the antepenult (kusākana, bīkusi, kitupīkilo; but kukēnta by rule 2); 7 disyllables: first syllable (būle, lēta, pīta, kōnu), unless closely bound to the preceding word, whose last syllable then takes the accent (letā bule); 8 mono…

sources.note: Sec. I.2 'Phonèmes supra-segmentaux' (p. 21): 'Il s'agit essentiellement de la durée ou longueur vocalique et de la tonalité.' I.2.1 contrastive vowel length with neutralisation (always long before NC and after C+glide, short word-finally); I.2.2 four tones (bas, haut, montant, descendant) with minimal pairs; I.2.3 syllable and mora. No mention of accent or stress anywhere in the suprasegmental section.
